idiom_name: CustomerDAO interface + JdbcCustomerDAO + DAOFactory over JDBC (the pattern's home form)
implementation_notes: Java is where the pattern was catalogued, and the classic form is hand-written: a CustomerDAO interface in domain terms, one implementation per store holding a DataSource (the preferred way to obtain connections), PreparedStatement calls and row-to-transfer-object mapping. What is library-provided is the access layer underneath - DriverManager, DataSource, Connection, PreparedStatement, ResultSet and SQLException ship with the JDK - so the DAO contributes domain vocabulary and error translation rather than plumbing. Keep the plain JDBC form when explicit SQL and full control are wanted; on modern stacks the template and ORM variants below remove most of the boilerplate while keeping the same interface.
pitfalls: A ResultSet is valid only while its Statement and Connection are open: map rows before returning and never declare a ResultSet or RowSet as the DAO's return type.
try-with-resources is not optional; a leaked Connection exhausts the pool and surfaces as an unrelated timeout later.
Catching SQLException in business code defeats the boundary - translate SQLState codes once, inside the DAO's own exception type.

variants.name: DAO over Spring JdbcTemplate/JdbcClient with a RowMapper
variants.implementation_notes: Spring's JdbcTemplate is the central delegate in the JDBC core package: it executes the workflow, iterating the ResultSet and translating SQLException into the framework's DataAccessException hierarchy, so the DAO keeps only SQL plus a RowMapper or extractor, and JdbcClient adds a fluent style on top. Choose it when the application already runs on Spring Framework 6+ (which requires Java 17) and the team wants explicit SQL without hand-written resource management; keep the classic JDBC variant when framework-neutral code or a non-Spring stack is required.
pitfalls: JdbcTemplate is thread-safe once configured, but opening your own Connection inside a callback escapes Spring's resource management and the surrounding transaction.
Spring's DataAccessException is already a vendor-agnostic, unchecked translation; re-wrapping it in a local exception loses that classification and can break rollback rules.

variants.name: DAO over a Jakarta Persistence EntityManager (ORM-mapped store)
variants.idiom_name: EntityManager find/persist plus JPQL or Criteria queries
variants.implementation_notes: With Jakarta Persistence the DAO thins out to a layer over EntityManager: rows are already mapped to entities, so methods call find/persist/merge, JPQL or the Criteria API, and the container (or an explicit unit of work) owns the transaction. Oracle's DAO chapter anticipated this as its automatic code-generation strategy: statements and mapping are derived from metadata instead of being written per aggregate. Prefer it when the domain maps cleanly and a mapper is acceptable; keep an explicit SQL DAO for reports and hot paths where the query shape must be controlled by hand.
pitfalls: em.find returns a managed instance held in the persistence context: returning entities to callers couples them to the session, so detach or map to transfer objects at the boundary.
Detached-entity merges, lazy loading outside a transaction and N+1 selects are ORM traps the DAO cannot hide once entity types appear in its signature.
